sources.news_title: DOJ Moves to Preemptively Block Certification of Alaska Senate Race
sources.text:
The U.S. Department of Justice is seeking to preemptively block certification of the Alaska U.S. Senate contest should the state certify “electoral results tainted by the inclusion” of liberal activist Daniel J. Sullivan, who is being propped up by left-wing Democrats due to sharing the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The two-term senator is seeking a third term in office and is one of four candidates in the race, along with former Democrat Rep. Mary Peltola, the liberal Sullivan, and Gerald Heikes.
The lawsuit, which was filed in federal court in Alaska on October 22, provides a lengthy list of exhibits detailing the extent of which left-wing interests have sought to confuse voters with identical names and signage. The Alaska Division of Elections initially kicked the liberal activist off the ballot, but his candidacy was reinstated by the Alaska Supreme Court.
The liberal activist Sullivan told the New York Times he voted for the Democrat nominee in the last three presidential elections and did not vote for the senator in his previous two campaigns. He said he backed Peltola in her 2022 and 2024 U.S. House bids and has donated to her and other Democrats, according to previous Breitbart News reporting.
Alaska uses a controversial ranked-choice voting process, in which voters are asked to rank their choices in each contest on the state’s ballot. Even small shifts in preference could play a role in the eventual winner of the race.
In addition to the state, the suit names Alaska Elections Division Director Carol Beecher, the state’s election boards, and the state Ballot Counting Review Board as defendants, CNBC reported on the matter.
“The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the filing reads.

sources.news_title: DOJ is suing to decertify Alaska's Senate race—but only if Republicans lose
sources.text:
The Department of Justice filed suit against the state of Alaska on Thursday, preemptively attempting to decertify the state’s election results—unless they win.
Their justification: Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, who served as Alaska’s House representative from 2022 to 2025, is running against two men named Dan Sullivan, and that could be pretty confusing for voters.
Dan S. Sullivan is the incumbent Republican senator; Dan J. Sullivan Jr. is a retired teacher and registered Republican running as an independent.
“Daniel J. Sullivan decided to run for Senator in 2026 as a Republican with
the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him,” the suit alleges. “The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.” If Peltola wins, the DOJ argued, the state should not certify the election results. 
The less well known Sullivan denies any ill intent. He decided to run, he told the New York Times in August, because he was unimpressed with the current Sen. Sullivan’s leadership; he felt his name would give him “an instant megaphone.”
The lawsuit telegraphs Donald Trump’s intention to intervene in the upcoming midterm elections, in which Democrats are broadly maintaining a polling lead. But legal experts doubt the suit will go anywhere.
“The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” wrote Notre Dame Law School professor Derek Muller. “It is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation.”
In that, the Alaska lawsuit would join other Trump-administration attempts to sway elections since the start of the President’s second term. According to the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan policy group, at least 34 federal district court decisions have temporarily halted or permanently blocked administration efforts to interfere in elections. That includes 22 judges appointed by Democratic presidents and 12 appointed by Republican presidents.
On Friday, Trump confirmed that the plan to sue Alaska came directly from his office.
“I’m the one who said do it,” Trump said to a group of reporters in Florida.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Can Trump block the Alaska Senate election?
Why the DOJ is suing over two Dan Sullivans running for Senate.
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is getting a head start on litigating the midterms.
What’s happening? The administration is asking a federal district court in Alaska to potentially block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate race, should incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, lose to his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola.
It’s the first major lawsuit of the 2026 midterms aimed at directly challenging the results, and very likely a sign of things to come after polls close on November 3.
What is the administration arguing? Sullivan is currently in a close race against Peltola, a former US representative who polls suggest may hold a slight lead. But the race is complicated by the presence of a second Dan Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot (no relation).
According to the lawsuit, which names Alaska’s state elections director and several state elections entities as defendants, the election could be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan.”
The suit asks that “Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” which it defines as a loss by the incumbent Sullivan in the event that the other Sullivan attracts enough votes to alter the outcome of the election.
What’s the context? The second Dan Sullivan’s appearance on the ballot has already been litigated. After he was initially disqualified from the ballot, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he should be included, and he finished third in the state’s August primary (the top four vote-getters appear on Alaska’s general election ballot).
How worried about this should I be? For now, not very. Trump filing lawsuits disputing election results was all but inevitable, even if it’s surprising to see him start this early.
None of that means he’ll succeed: Trump and his allies filed dozens of election lawsuits in 2020 and were largely laughed out of court. (Plus, this particular lawsuit has been assigned to a judge appointed by President Barack Obama.)

sources.news_title: Alaskans, legal experts condemn federal lawsuit as attempt to invalidate the vote in U.S. Senate race
sources.text:
A range of legal experts and Alaskans decried a Trump administration lawsuit filed Thursday seeking to block certification of the state’s U.S. Senate election if the president’s preferred candidate, Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, loses the race.
The lawsuit seeks a court order preventing state election officials from declaring Sullivan’s Democratic opponent, former Congresswoman Mary Peltola, the winner of the Nov. 3 contest if a candidate who shares the incumbent’s first and last name, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan of Petersburg, wins a share of the vote. Specifically, the lawsuit seeks to block a Peltola win “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”
“This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan’s allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he’ll lose the seat,” said Harry Child, Peltola’s campaign spokesman.
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign, expressed confidence in his reelection but said by text Friday “we’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course.”
Alaska’s Senate race has been closely watched nationwide as one of a handful that could determine control of the chamber. More than 30,000 Alaskans had already cast early and absentee ballots as of Friday morning, according to the Division of Elections, and the Sept. 10 deadline to challenge primary results passed more than a month ago.
President Trump has repeatedly derided the Petersburg Sullivan as a “hoax” candidate put forward by Democrats to siphon votes away from the incumbent. The Petersburg Sullivan has denied any connection to the Democratic Party and insisted that he’s running because he’s dissatisfied with Sen. Sullivan’s record. Contacted by Petersburg public radio station KFSK Friday, he declined to comment.
The president said he had personally directed the Justice Department to pursue the lawsuit.
“I’m the one who said, ‘do it,’” Trump told reporters during a stop in Florida Friday afternoon.
The Alaska Department of Law, which defends state agencies in court, said it was reviewing the complaint and did not have an immediate comment on the merits of the lawsuit. Spokesperson Sam Curtis said the Department of Law and Division of Elections were “focused on running the ongoing election and giving voters confidence their votes will count.” That includes making sure voters aren’t confused by their choices, he said.
The lawsuit represents a baseless effort by the Trump administration to interfere in the state’s elections, a range of legal experts said Friday.
State Sen. Bill Wielechowski, an Anchorage Democrat who’s led efforts to reform the state’s election system, said the suit was “a political stunt” with “zero merit to it.”
“They’re throwing the kitchen sink out, doing everything they can to try to tip the scales in Sen. Dan Sullivan’s favor,” Wielechowski said.
The Division of Elections sought to remove the Petersburg Sullivan from the ballot ahead of the August primary, arguing he joined the race intending to confuse voters. But the Alaska Supreme Court in June ordered the Division of Elections to place the retired teacher on the ballot. The justices said the state could instead list them differently, to alleviate voter confusion.
The Petersburg candidate advanced to the general election after placing third in the August primary with 2.5% of the vote.
The Division of Elections lists the Petersburg candidate as “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.” without a party affiliation and the senator, Dan S. Sullivan, as the incumbent Republican.
State Rep. Andrew Gray, an Anchorage Democrat who chairs the state House Judiciary Committee, said on social media that many of the primary votes for the Petersburg teacher were “protest votes against Mary Peltola.”
“It is very clear which is which. No one is making a mistake,” Gray said.
Former Republican state Rep. Jesse Sumner of Wasilla said he, too, was skeptical the same-name candidate’s presence on the ballot would damage the incumbent’s chances of winning.
“I don’t think people are likely to confuse him with the incumbent senator,” Sumner said.
David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney overseeing voting rights enforcement who now heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said the Justice Department lawsuit is an unprecedented intervention by the federal government.
“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” Becker said. “The DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy, as there is no legitimate enforcement of federal law here, and it raises serious concerns about political interference.”
Another former Justice Department attorney, Justin Levitt, said he expected courts to reject the suit.
“There is no path for DOJ to block certification of an election result based on any notion that a candidate shouldn’t have been running,” he said. “That’s not a thing, and courts won’t give it the time of day.”
Libby Bakalar, a former state assistant attorney general, said on social media the suit was “laughably bad, almost to the point of sanctionably frivolous.”
But Wielechowski, the Democratic state senator, said he’s worried Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s administration might not faithfully defend the state from the Trump administration lawsuit. After all, state officials initially sought to remove the Petersburg Sullivan from the ballot, he said.
“I am very, very concerned that you’re seeing a highly politicized administration that is going to do everything that it can to try to tip the scales in favor of the candidates that they would like to see in office,” Wielechowski said.
Republican Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, the elected official who heads the Division of Elections, did not immediately return requests for comment
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

sources.news_title: Trump Orders DOJ to Sue Red State to Block Senate Election Certification if GOP Loses — and He’s Bragging About It
sources.text:
Donald Trump is taking credit for ordering the Justice Department to sue Alaska in an extraordinary attempt to stop the state from certifying its U.S. Senate election results if the Republican incumbent loses.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters Friday, openly acknowledging his role in the lawsuit.
The administration claims that having two candidates named Daniel Sullivan on the ballot could confuse voters and potentially hurt Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan’s chances against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.
But the remedy the DOJ is seeking goes far beyond raising concerns about ballot confusion. The department wants a court order preventing Alaska from certifying the election results if the Republican incumbent does not win.
The Justice Department argues that voters might accidentally cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan instead of the sitting senator, Daniel S. Sullivan. Government attorneys claim that if votes cast for the second candidate had instead gone to the incumbent, Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system would have produced a Republican victory.
The DOJ has described the rival candidate’s campaign as “frivolous” and argued that Alaska should not certify results potentially affected by voter confusion.
But there is a major problem with that argument: Alaska’s courts have already examined the claim that the second Sullivan was running to confuse voters.
In June, the Alaska Division of Elections removed Daniel J. Sullivan from the primary ballot, saying his candidacy was intended to mislead voters. He appealed, and an Anchorage Superior Court judge overturned the decision, finding that the claim was not supported by a preponderance of the evidence. The ruling was upheld on appeal, and the state did not take the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.
The primary results showed Mary Peltola finishing first with 49.5% of the vote, followed by incumbent Dan S. Sullivan with 41.4% and Daniel J. Sullivan with 2.5%.
Now, with Peltola polling closely alongside the Republican incumbent, the Trump administration is asking a federal court to intervene in the election before November’s voting is even over.
Trump made no effort to distance himself from the move.
“I’m the one that said do it,” he said proudly in remarks reported Friday.
That public admission is especially striking because the lawsuit comes amid broader concerns about the administration’s willingness to intervene in election administration ahead of the midterms.
The lawsuit follows a warning from Trump’s attorney general.
Just one day before the Alaska lawsuit was filed, Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out the Justice Department intervening to stop states from certifying election results.
Blanche described hypothetical scenarios in which federal intervention might occur, while insisting that the department had no plan to improperly interfere with elections.
But he also declined to promise that the DOJ would never intervene under any circumstances.
Days earlier, Blanche — Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer — had openly rejected the idea that the Justice Department should operate independently of the White House.
“There was this misperception that there’s this separation and independence between the Department of Justice and the White House,” Blanche told a New York Post podcast. “I don’t.”
Now, Trump’s own admission that he ordered the Alaska lawsuit is adding fuel to questions about the relationship between the White House and the nation’s top law enforcement agency.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, called the lawsuit an “unprecedented intervention by the federal government.”
“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” Becker said.
Becker added that the DOJ’s intervention so close to Election Day raises serious concerns about political interference.
Former Alaska state elections attorney Libby Bakalar called the government’s argument “laughably bad,” while Notre Dame election law professor Derek Muller described it as one of the worst arguments he had seen.
The campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola also condemned the lawsuit. Harry Child, a spokesperson for Alaskans for Mary, called it a “despicable political threat to overturn an election.”
The campaign accused allies of Sen. Sullivan of trying to suppress Alaskans’ votes because the Republican faces a competitive race. Those are the campaign’s allegations, not established findings about the lawsuit’s motives.
A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said it would “let the DOJ complaint run its course,” adding that Alaskans could judge the senator on his record.
With control of the Senate at stake, the fight over Alaska’s election is becoming a test of how far the Trump administration is willing to go when a competitive race threatens a Republican incumbent.

The U.S. Justice Department on Thursday sued to pre-emptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its U.S. Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses by a narrow margin, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
The lawsuit signals the willingness of President Donald Trump’s administration to contest the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the U.S. Congress.
Trump’s administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including both Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
Control of the U.S. Senate could come down to Alaska, where incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan is running a closely contested race against Democrat Mary Peltola.

A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that the agency is taking “necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit Thursday in federal court in Alaska to block state officials from certifying the results of the U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses next month.
The complaint argues that the presence on the ballot of another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan is a purposeful attempt to mislead voters and thwart the will of the electorate.
“Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Daniel J. Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan, and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity,” DOJ wrote.

Alaska has rank-choice voting, which permits the top four vote-getters in the primary to advance to the general election. If no candidate receives an outright majority in the general election, voters’ second-choice selections are factored in until someone reaches over 50 percent of the tally.

sources.news_title: Voters react to DOJ lawsuit raising questions about Alaska Senate race
sources.text:
The U.S. Justice Department has filed a lawsuit that could affect certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race. The Trump Administration argues that two candidates with the same name on the ballot could confuse voters.
The DOJ lawsuit could potentially prevent Alaska from certifying Mary Peltola as the winner of the U.S. Senate race.
The controversy stems from the similar names of Dan J. Sullivan and incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, and concerns that voters could be confused.
Hillary Morgan says she had no trouble telling the candidates apart and questions why the lawsuit was filed.
"I don't really understand what grounds there could be for a lawsuit or even why you would want to bring one up unless you just want to make sure your guy won."
Gloria Johnson also says the names didn't confuse her and believes the legal process should run its course, saying, “We have to trust in our justice system and the Constitution that's been around for a long time. And some people are willing to abide by what the Constitution says”
Justine Newsom understands the reasoning behind the lawsuit but says she can also see both sides.
"The way that they did it, I would say yes. But I also understand why they did it the way they did it, so it could go either way."
Linda Simmons says she's disappointed with the situation.
“I think it's sad that it has come to that. But that's politics, right?”
The lawsuit doesn't mean Peltola automatically loses.
The DOJ is asking a judge to step in if votes for the other Dan Sullivan could have affected the outcome. It would be up to the judge to decide whether to block Alaska from certifying the results.
President Donald Trump says he personally directed the Justice Department to file the lawsuit.
Speaking to reporters in Florida, Trump said Democrats recruited Republican candidate Dan J. Sullivan to confuse voters with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, who shares his name.

The Volokh Conspiracy
Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent
Trump Sues to Block Alaska Senate Election Results Because of Potential Voter "Confusion"
The administration claims voters might be confused between two candidates named "Dan Sullivan."
Today, the Trump Justice Department filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block Alaska Senate election results on the grounds they might be influenced by voter "confusion" between incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan and a separate Republican candidate with a very similar name (Dan L. Sullivan). I previously wrote the issues raised by the two Dan Sullivans here. As I pointed out in the earlier post, there is no legal basis for overturning congressional election results based on voter confusion, and any such action would likely violate the First Amendment. See also this analysis by election law specialist Rick Hasen.
I would add that any such federal action also runs afoul of states' primary authority over election procedures. The Elections Clause of the Constitution gives states primary authority over "The Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives," subject to Congress' power to modify these rules by legislation. Congress has not enacted any statute allowing overturning of election results based on possible "voter confusion."
If "voter confusion" were a legitimate reason to overturn election results, that would imperil a great many election winners, as voter ignorance - and exploitation thereof by candidates - is a widespread and longstanding problem. I covered some of these points in my previous post about the two Dan Sullivans:
Donald Trump is a particularly egregious example, going all the way back to his first campaign in 2016, and more recently with his lies about the 2020 election and other issues. But more conventional politicians also often resort to lies and deception, even if not to the same degree. President Obama, for example, famously lied when he claimed that, under the Affordable Care Act, "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it." That deception won the 2013 Politifact Lie of the Year award. But it still helped Obama get reelected in 2012. I am not sure exploiting voter confusion about names is any worse than exploiting their ignorance about policy issues like crime, immigration, and health care….
Ultimately, both exploitation of voter confusion about names and other deceptions used in campaigns seek to exploit widespread voter ignorance. Because of the combination of "rational ignorance" (lack of incentive to seek out political information) and "rational irrationality" (lack of incentive to engage in unbiased evaluation), most voters know little about government and public policy, and often do a poor job of evaluating the information they do know. This makes them vulnerable to deception and manipulation, and incentivizes politicians to lie and otherwise distort the truth.
Voter confusion about candidates with similar names is just another example of this broader problem….
There is no easy solution to the problem of voter ignorance. But I assess a range of possible options in my 2023 article on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in my earlier book Democracy and Political Ignorance. I believe the best approach is to make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and evaluate it wisely are much better. But I recognize that any effective approach will take time, and there may be no one fix that is sufficient by itself. We may need to pursue multiple strategies. In the meantime, voters are likely to continue to be ignorant and confused about a variety of issues, and politicians and interest groups are likely to keep on exploiting that.
Many of these other voter ignorance problems are far worse than any potential confusion between candidates with similar names, a problem that only comes up relatively rarely.

By NICHOLAS RICCARDI, Associated Press
President Donald Trump’s administration has taken its first step to block the results of a midterm election, and it’s all about the fact that there are two Dan Sullivans on the Alaska Senate ballot.
One of them is a Republican and ally of the president. The other is a retired school teacher whom Republicans accuse of being a Democratic plant to siphon away votes.
Trump said Friday that he directed the Justice Department to file its lawsuit.
What is going on? Here’s an explanation:
Why is there a lawsuit over this?
The campaign is likely to be decided by only a few thousand votes, and it could determine which party controls the Senate. So the stakes are high, and Republicans worry that voters will get confused and accidentally vote for the wrong Sullivan.
That’s why Republicans have been trying to get the second Dan Sullivan — hereafter known as Daniel J. Sullivan — thrown off the ballot for months. The lawsuit went all the way to the Alaska Supreme Court, but Republicans lost.
Republicans think the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic dirty trick. But Daniel J. Sullivan, who lives in the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, says he is running of his own accord.
Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation. Former Rep. Mary Peltola is the Democratic candidate.
So the Trump administration is filing in federal court to try to block certification of the election if its Dan Sullivan — the senator — loses.
“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan,” the lawsuit said, “the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election.”
Trump said of the lawsuit: “I’m the one who said do it.”
Will this work?
The lawsuit is essentially a placeholder and only becomes an issue after Election Day if the incumbent loses.
Even if that happens, legal experts say it has no chance of success. The suit cites a clause in the preamble to the National Voter Registration Act that says states must “protect the integrity” of elections. It says that gives federal courts grounds to overturn elections which, under the U.S. Constitution, are entirely state affairs. But that vague turn of phrase probably isn’t enough for any judge to try to overrule the will of the voters, experts say.
Technically, the lawsuit only asks the court to block certification until an investigation determines whether enough voters were fooled by the two Sullivans to have swung the election. It doesn’t explain how that would happen, which seems like a big issue given that votes are supposed to be confidential.
Why does this matter?
Dirty tricks and voter confusion are nothing new in American politics. In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
What is new is that the Justice Department is trying to block an election result. Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins
The move is the latest attempt by the President to support incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan against a Democratic challenger
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at a rally featuring President Donald Trump on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla. On Oct. 22, Trump ordered the U.S. Department of Justice to file a lawsuit that would prohibit anyone but Sullivan from being certified as the winner of the U.S. Senate election. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
This article is developing and may be updated.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed suit against the Alaska Division of Elections late Thursday, seeking to block the division from certifying the result of the state’s U.S. Senate election if the Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, wins.
President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday in Florida that he ordered the lawsuit be filed.
“I’m the one that said, ‘do it,’” he said.
Peltola is the leading opponent to incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and polls show her with a small lead over Sullivan, but the race also includes two other people — Republican Gerald Heikes of Palmer and undeclared candidate Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg.
In the complaint, the Department of Justice claims that Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy is “frivolous,” and was intended solely to confuse voters and benefit Peltola.
Until there is an investigation to determine the extent of that confusion, the Department of Justice argues, Alaska should not be permitted to certify the result of the ongoing Senate election.
Legal experts immediately dismissed the federal argument as bunk.
‘A sad and scary sight’
Under the U.S. Constitution, states have authority over their own elections. The federal claim is based on the preamble to the National Voter Registration Act, which states in part that the law is intended “to protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
In an immediate analysis posted online, Notre Dame Law School election law professor Derek Muller said, “the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”
In addition to being poorly argued, it was poorly written, he said, noting that one paragraph is missing a verb that would ask the court to take action.
Libby Bakalar is a former Alaska state elections attorney who frequently speaks against the Trump administration. On social media Friday morning, she said the federal argument “is laughably bad, almost to the point of sanctionably frivolous. Watching MAGA on the ropes like this in court up here is a sad and scary sight.”
The case has been referred to Judge Sharon Gleason, an Obama appointee who is the most senior of the two judges in the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.
Trump says he made the call to file the lawsuit
In numerous prior interviews, Dan J. Sullivan has said that his candidacy was motivated by dissatisfaction with Sen. Sullivan, and that he is not linked to the Democratic Party or Peltola’s campaign.
Democratic officials have said the same thing.
But that hasn’t stopped Trump and Sen. Sullivan — as well as other Republicans — from accusing both Peltola and Petersburg Sullivan of fraud.
Trump and other administration officials hinted throughout the summer and fall that they were working to bring a criminal case against Dan J. Sullivan, who was a registered Republican in July. He’s now listed as “undeclared,” an independent, in state voter files.
Thursday’s filing does not name him as a defendant.
The listed attorneys for the Department of Justice are Stanley E. Woodward, an associate attorney general in Washington, D.C. and E. Bryan Wilson, an assistant U.S. attorney in Anchorage.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman was at Trump’s rally in Wasilla this month.
“I told him — I just shook his hand, took a picture — I said I hope you’re going to make sure there’s no cheating, because any place you have rank(ed) choice, you have damn bad cheating. And we can’t let that happen. So, we’re going to defend the integrity of Alaska’s elections,” Trump said at the Oct. 13 event.
Legal action isn’t expected until after the election
By phone, Muller said he doesn’t expect the federal government’s case to advance until after Election Day, if at all.
That’s because the lawsuit is based on possible confusion by Dan J. Sullivan voters. If Dan S. Sullivan wins, any confusion didn’t matter. If Peltola wins by a margin bigger than the number of votes for Dan S. Sullivan, the confusion wasn’t decisive.
“The court’s going to sit and wait till after the election to adjudicate it. Presumably, anyway,” Muller said.
Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting, any hypothetical confused voter would simply have to rank both Sullivans to have their vote count the way they want.
“If there’s any confusion, a lot of that is mitigated by ranked choice voting … it’s really not going to affect the outcome of the election simply because of the way ranked choice voting is designed to work,” he said.
Even in a scenario where Judge Gleason declines to dismiss the case and Peltola wins by a smaller margin than the number of first-choice votes for Dan S. Sullivan, Muller said, the federal government would have to find those Dan S. Sullivan voters and prove they were confused.
“It’s an impossible evidentiary question at the end of the day,” he said.
Tom Lamb is a former Republican U.S. Senate candidate who argued in favor of Dan J. Sullivan in an Alaska Supreme Court case earlier this year. He’s preparing to do so in the newly filed federal case too, and said there’s no way to prove what the federal government wants to.
“If I say I voted for Sullivan Jr. and I made a mistake, there’s no way of verifying that,” he said.
Peltola or her campaign may intervene in suit
Reached by email Friday morning, Dan J. Sullivan declined immediate comment, saying the lawsuit came as a surprise and he was still analyzing it. He did not answer additional messages Friday seeking an interview.
The Beacon contacted the Division of Elections and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom early Friday and repeatedly throughout the day. Sam Curtis, a spokesman for the Department of Law, said Friday afternoon that the division is “focused on running the ongoing election and giving voters confidence that their votes will count.”
The Department of Law represents the division and lieutenant governor in court.
“The complaint is being reviewed, and we do not have any comment on the litigation,” he said.
A person affiliated with Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said Friday morning that he did not ask the Department of Justice to file the lawsuit and that he was surprised by the act.
Nate Adams, campaign spokesman for Sullivan, said by email, “We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course. Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he’ll keep building on for the next six years.”
The chair of the Alaska Republican Party, Carmela Warfield, did not return a text message or phone call seeking comment Friday.
Harry Child, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign, replied to questions by text message and implied that the campaign may intervene in the lawsuit.
“This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan’s allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he’ll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans’ expense for over a decade,” Child said. “We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections.”
Asked his opinion, Alaska Democratic Party chair Eric Croft said, “Dan Sullivan is scared he’ll lose and that’s why he’s looking to any corrupt, desperate method to win.”
Review of primary election results indicates few voters were confused
Alaska’s state courts have already argued — and decided — Dan J. Sullivan’s eligibility as a candidate. In June, the Alaska Division of Elections struck him from the primary ballot, saying his candidacy was “for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters.”
He appealed that decision, and in late June, an Anchorage Superior Court judge overturned the division’s decision.
“The director’s assertion that Mr. Sullivan seeks to confuse or misguide voters is not supported by a preponderance of evidence,” wrote Judge Thomas Matthews in a 32-page analysis.
The state appealed, but the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the trial court’s decision on June 29. It has not yet published a full explanation of its decision.
The state did not seek an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
After that decision, Peltola, Dan J. Sullivan, Dan S. Sullivan and 13 other candidates appeared on the primary ballot in August. Peltola finished first, with 49.5% of the vote, followed by Dan S. Sullivan with 41.4% and Dan J. Sullivan with 2.5%.
The fourth-place finisher, Democratic candidate David Leslie, withdrew from the election, an act that promoted Heikes into the final four with 1.1% of the vote.
A subsequent review of the results by the Anchorage Press found a large proportion of votes for Dan J. Sullivan came from left-leaning districts, indicating that Democratic-inclined voters — rather than confused Republicans — put the Petersburg man into the general election.
“I feel pretty vindicated that it seems to prove that there was very little, if any, voter confusion between the senator and myself,” Dan J. Sullivan told local radio station KFSK-FM after the result.

Trump’s DOJ sues over Alaska Senate race, expanding preelection legal fights • West Virginia Watch
sources.text:
Trump’s DOJ sues over Alaska Senate race, expanding preelection legal fights
Competing signs in the same Anchorage, Alaska yard, seen Aug. 7, 2026, support the candidates for U.S. Senate in Alaska: incumbent Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and challenger Mary Peltola, a Democrat. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
The U.S. Department of Justice is stepping up its legal campaign over the midterm elections, suing Alaska over its U.S. Senate election and appealing a lawsuit against suspected noncitizen voters in California.
Election law experts have cast doubt on the strength of the cases, criticizing them as performative.
The Justice Department sued Alaska election officials late Thursday in a preemptive attempt to stop the state from certifying the results of its Senate election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting method, the Republican incumbent loses by a smaller margin than the votes earned by another candidate of the same name.
Separately, the Justice Department appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals a lawsuit seeking to prevent California election officials from counting the ballots of approximately 20,000 voters it says are likely noncitizens unless they can prove their citizenship. The DOJ had demanded a district court decision by Thursday.
Collectively, the Justice Department’s actions signal an expanding legal effort to assert authority over voting as Election Day approaches. President Donald Trump faces political peril in the midterms, with Democrats all but certain to launch investigations into his administration if they retake the House or Senate.
The Trump administration’s past attempts to influence how states run elections largely failed, with the U.S. Supreme Court blocking proposed restrictions on mail ballots and federal judges dismissing DOJ lawsuits to obtain states’ sensitive voter data. But in the waning days before the midterm elections, federal officials are again ramping up election-related activity.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump, speaking to reporters on Friday, said of the Alaska lawsuit.
Another Dan Sullivan suit
The Alaska lawsuit came hours after U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out efforts to block states from certifying their elections. Speaking to reporters after an unrelated event in Virginia, Blanche said it wasn’t the DOJ’s intention to “improperly interfere” with election certifications even as he left room for his department to act.
“I mean, is there any scenario? Yes, of course there’s scenarios that we could all come up with, hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?” Blanche said.
The Alaska Division of Elections and the Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
In the Alaska Senate race, Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and his supporters have cast Dan J. Sullivan, also a Republican, as a spoiler in a competitive race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
State officials initially kept Dan J. Sullivan off the August primary ballot but the Alaska Supreme Court overturned the decision. He finished third, with 2.5% of the vote, qualifying for the four-way general election.
Trump had previewed a possible lawsuit earlier in the week. On Truth Social, the president on Wednesday called the Senate race in Alaska “totally confusing” and slammed Dan J. Sullivan’s presence.
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” Trump wrote.
Experts skeptical
Early expert reaction to the Justice Department’s complaint has been sharply critical. The complaint cites the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act, which says one of its purposes is “to protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
Writing in Election Law Blog, Derek Muller, a professor of law at the University of Notre Dame focused on elections, called the legal argument “one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”
“Some, in a panic, might react that the Department is trying to deny certification of an election in a state. Of course that’s what the Department is trying to do. But the legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” Muller wrote.
California noncitizen case appealed
In California, Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Hamill filed a notice of appeal in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over alleged noncitizen voters just three days after the the DOJ requested a temporary restraining order to halt ballot counting for individuals on the list of 20,000.
Hamill wrote that the DOJ was interpreting U.S. District Court Judge David Carter’s silence as a denial of its request.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, had only taken on the case a day earlier and had set a hearing for Oct. 27. Earlier this year, he became the first federal judge in the country to rule against the Justice Department’s lawsuits attempting to force states to turn over sensitive voter data.
On Friday, the Justice Department filed a new motion asking Carter to block the ballot counting and requested a ruling by noon Pacific time.
In that filing, Hamill wrote that “every minute” of ballot processing that occurs without setting aside ballots of suspected noncitizens dilutes the votes of U.S. citizens.
Case ‘exceedingly weak,’ critics say
Critics of the Justice Department’s actions argue the time crunch is largely of its own making.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, noted during a press call Thursday that the DOJ didn’t file its lawsuit until more than a week after California began mailing ballots — and then several more days to seek a temporary restraining order.
“I think this case is exceedingly weak,” said Becker, who worked as a senior trial attorney in the Justice Department’s Voting Section during the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations.
Attorneys for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have both asked Carter to dismiss the lawsuit.
Logan’s legal team on Wednesday wrote that Los Angeles County hasn’t changed how it conducts elections. What’s changed, they wrote, was the federal government’s posture.
“Weeks before Election Day, the United States asks this Court to intrude on the administration of an election,” Logan’s lawyers wrote.

The Justice Department has filed suit against Alaska election officials, seeking to block the results of November’s U.S. Senate election from being certified unless incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan wins — a controversial move President Donald Trump claimed credit for.
In papers filed in federal court, attorneys for the DOJ argued the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot could mislead supporters of the sitting senator, Daniel S. Sullivan.
“For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan,” the filing says.
“To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the suit says.
The Trump administration is seeking a court order blocking the results from being certified “if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”
Trump told reporters Friday that he directed the suit to be filed.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump said, calling Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy “a disgrace.”
The filing by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said the action was brought “to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.”
Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee in the Senate race, blasted the move in a post on X, saying, “This is the corruption AK is fed up with,” and that Sullivan is “using his DC allies to try to keep himself in power and put his own interests ahead of Alaskans.”
Sullivan’s Senate office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit, nor did his campaign when asked about the suit and Peltola’s post.
Alaska’s Division of Elections said in a statement that it is reviewing the complaint and is “focused on running the ongoing election and giving voter’s confidence that their votes will count.”
“This also includes assisting voters and avoiding voter confusion — whether through the information in the Official Election Pamphlet, asking questions of a poll worker, or bringing others to assist you with voting as permitted by law,” the department said.
The Trump administration filed the suit Thursday, the same day Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that “it is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.”

The Justice Department sued Alaska election officials late Thursday in a preemptive attempt to stop the state from certifying the results of its Senate election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting method, the Republican incumbent loses by a smaller margin than the votes earned by another candidate of the same name.
Separately, the Justice Department appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals a lawsuit seeking to prevent California election officials from counting the ballots of approximately 20,000 voters it says are likely noncitizens unless they can prove their citizenship. The DOJ had demanded a district court decision by Thursday.
Collectively, the Justice Department’s actions signal an expanding legal effort to assert authority over voting as Election Day approaches. President Donald Trump faces political peril in the midterms, with Democrats all but certain to launch investigations into his administration if they retake the House or Senate.
The Trump administration’s past attempts to influence how states run elections largely failed, with the U.S. Supreme Court blocking proposed restrictions on mail ballots and federal judges dismissing DOJ lawsuits to obtain states’ sensitive voter data. But in the waning days before the midterm elections, federal officials are again ramping up election-related activity.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump, speaking to reporters on Friday, said of the Alaska lawsuit.
Another Dan Sullivan suit
The Alaska lawsuit came hours after U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out efforts to block states from certifying their elections. Speaking to reporters after an unrelated event in Virginia, Blanche said it wasn’t the DOJ’s intention to “improperly interfere” with election certifications even as he left room for his department to act.
“I mean, is there any scenario? Yes, of course there’s scenarios that we could all come up with, hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?” Blanche said.
The Alaska Division of Elections and the Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
In the Alaska Senate race, Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and his supporters have cast Dan J. Sullivan, also a Republican, as a spoiler in a competitive race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
State officials initially kept Dan J. Sullivan off the August primary ballot but the Alaska Supreme Court overturned the decision. He finished third, with 2.5% of the vote, qualifying for the four-way general election.
Trump had previewed a possible lawsuit earlier in the week. On Truth Social, the president on Wednesday called the Senate race in Alaska “totally confusing” and slammed Dan J. Sullivan’s presence.
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” Trump wrote.
Experts skeptical
Early expert reaction to the Justice Department’s complaint has been sharply critical. The complaint cites the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act, which says one of its purposes is “to protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
Writing in Election Law Blog, Derek Muller, a professor of law at the University of Notre Dame focused on elections, called the legal argument “one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”
“Some, in a panic, might react that the Department is trying to deny certification of an election in a state. Of course that’s what the Department is trying to do. But the legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” Muller wrote.

In California, Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Hamill filed a notice of appeal in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over alleged noncitizen voters just three days after the the DOJ requested a temporary restraining order to halt ballot counting for individuals on the list of 20,000.
Hamill wrote that the DOJ was interpreting U.S. District Court Judge David Carter’s silence as a denial of its request.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, had only taken on the case a day earlier and had set a hearing for Oct. 27. Earlier this year, he became the first federal judge in the country to rule against the Justice Department’s lawsuits attempting to force states to turn over sensitive voter data.
On Friday, the Justice Department filed a new motion asking Carter to block the ballot counting and requested a ruling by noon Pacific time.
In that filing, Hamill wrote that “every minute” of ballot processing that occurs without setting aside ballots of suspected noncitizens dilutes the votes of U.S. citizens.

Critics of the Justice Department’s actions argue the time crunch is largely of its own making.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, noted during a press call Thursday that the DOJ didn’t file its lawsuit until more than a week after California began mailing ballots — and then several more days to seek a temporary restraining order.
“I think this case is exceedingly weak,” said Becker, who worked as a senior trial attorney in the Justice Department’s Voting Section during the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations.
Attorneys for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have both asked Carter to dismiss the lawsuit.
Logan’s legal team on Wednesday wrote that Los Angeles County hasn’t changed how it conducts elections. What’s changed, they wrote, was the federal government’s posture.
“Weeks before Election Day, the United States asks this Court to intrude on the administration of an election,” Logan’s lawyers wrote.

The U.S. Department of Justice is stepping up its legal campaign over the midterm elections, suing Alaska over its U.S. Senate election and appealing a lawsuit against suspected noncitizen voters in California.
Election law experts have cast doubt on the strength of the cases, criticizing them as performative.
The Justice Department sued Alaska election officials late Thursday in a preemptive attempt to stop the state from certifying the results of its Senate election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting method, the Republican incumbent loses by a smaller margin than the votes earned by another candidate of the same name.
Separately, the Justice Department appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals a lawsuit seeking to prevent California election officials from counting the ballots of approximately 20,000 voters it says are likely noncitizens unless they can prove their citizenship. The DOJ had demanded a district court decision by Thursday.
Collectively, the Justice Department’s actions signal an expanding legal effort to assert authority over voting as Election Day approaches. President Donald Trump faces political peril in the midterms, with Democrats all but certain to launch investigations into his administration if they retake the House or Senate.
The Trump administration’s past attempts to influence how states run elections largely failed, with the U.S. Supreme Court blocking proposed restrictions on mail ballots and federal judges dismissing DOJ lawsuits to obtain states’ sensitive voter data. But in the waning days before the midterm elections, federal officials are again ramping up election-related activity.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump, speaking to reporters on Friday, said of the Alaska lawsuit.
Another Dan Sullivan suit
The Alaska lawsuit came hours after U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out efforts to block states from certifying their elections. Speaking to reporters after an unrelated event in Virginia, Blanche said it wasn’t the DOJ’s intention to “improperly interfere” with election certifications even as he left room for his department to act.
“I mean, is there any scenario? Yes, of course there’s scenarios that we could all come up with, hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?” Blanche said.
The Alaska Division of Elections and the Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
In the Alaska Senate race, Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and his supporters have cast Dan J. Sullivan, also a Republican, as a spoiler in a competitive race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
State officials initially kept Dan J. Sullivan off the August primary ballot but the Alaska Supreme Court overturned the decision. He finished third, with 2.5% of the vote, qualifying for the four-way general election.
Trump had previewed a possible lawsuit earlier in the week. On Truth Social, the president on Wednesday called the Senate race in Alaska “totally confusing” and slammed Dan J. Sullivan’s presence.
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” Trump wrote.
Experts skeptical
Early expert reaction to the Justice Department’s complaint has been sharply critical. The complaint cites the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act, which says one of its purposes is “to protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
Writing in Election Law Blog, Derek Muller, a professor of law at the University of Notre Dame focused on elections, called the legal argument “one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”
“Some, in a panic, might react that the Department is trying to deny certification of an election in a state. Of course that’s what the Department is trying to do. But the legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” Muller wrote.
California noncitizen case appealed
In California, Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Hamill filed a notice of appeal in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over alleged noncitizen voters just three days after the the DOJ requested a temporary restraining order to halt ballot counting for individuals on the list of 20,000.
Hamill wrote that the DOJ was interpreting U.S. District Court Judge David Carter’s silence as a denial of its request.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, had only taken on the case a day earlier and had set a hearing for Oct. 27. Earlier this year, he became the first federal judge in the country to rule against the Justice Department’s lawsuits attempting to force states to turn over sensitive voter data.
On Friday, the Justice Department filed a new motion asking Carter to block the ballot counting and requested a ruling by noon Pacific time.
In that filing, Hamill wrote that “every minute” of ballot processing that occurs without setting aside ballots of suspected noncitizens dilutes the votes of U.S. citizens.
Case ‘exceedingly weak,’ critics say
Critics of the Justice Department’s actions argue the time crunch is largely of its own making.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, noted during a press call Thursday that the DOJ didn’t file its lawsuit until more than a week after California began mailing ballots — and then several more days to seek a temporary restraining order.
“I think this case is exceedingly weak,” said Becker, who worked as a senior trial attorney in the Justice Department’s Voting Section during the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations.
Attorneys for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have both asked Carter to dismiss the lawsuit.
Logan’s legal team on Wednesday wrote that Los Angeles County hasn’t changed how it conducts elections. What’s changed, they wrote, was the federal government’s posture.
“Weeks before Election Day, the United States asks this Court to intrude on the administration of an election,” Logan’s lawyers wrote.

sources.news_title: Trump DOJ sues to block Alaska US Senate results if Republican incumbent loses
sources.text:
The Trump administration has preemptively filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate election if the Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in the critical contest which could decide the balance of power in the Senate.
The lawsuit represents the latest attempt of the Trump Justice Department to insert itself in the administration of elections, running up against the minimal role the Constitution gives the Executive Branch. It alleges that a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could confuse voters and wants a court to potentially delay the certification of the election if the incumbent is defeated but would have won if “all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan” had “been cast instead for Senator Sullivan.”
President Donald Trump took credit for the legal challenge.
“Well, I’m the one that said ‘do it,’” Trump told reporters in Florida on Friday when asked about the lawsuit. The president has regularly complained about the presence of the non-incumbent Sullivan on the ballot.
The lawsuit is based on a “strange and unusual” legal theory, said Derek Muller, an election law professor at Notre Dame Law School. It’s also unclear, he said, how a court could intervene in the way the DOJ proposes.
The battle for control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where there has been little reliable polling but where Dan S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, and Democrat Mary Peltola have campaigned in a close race. Democrats need to net four seats in November to win the Senate, and Alaska is one of several Republican-held states that Democrats are hoping to flip.
The presence of the second Sullivan has brought additional controversy to the race and has already been a source of litigation, as Republicans have alleged he is running a spoiler candidacy designed to confuse voters.
Daniel J. Sullivan is a registered Republican, but state election officials listed him on the ballot without a party affiliation. Sen. Sullivan is labeled on the ballot as “Registered Republican” and “incumbent.”
In the primary, the incumbent Dan Sullivan won 68,726 votes. Daniel J. Sullivan won 4,107.
Trump this month also held a rally in Wasilla, Alaska.
“It’s just cheating,” he said of the ballot having two Dan Sullivans. “They found a guy named Dan Sullivan. They put him up to get a little confused.”
Nate Adams, a spokesman for Sen. Sullivan, said the incumbent will “let the DOJ complaint run its course.”
“Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he’ll keep building on for the next six years,” Adams added.
“This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election,” said Peltola spokesperson Harry Child. “We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections.”

The lawsuit points to the preface of a federal law setting guardrails on states’ voter registration procedures that protects the “integrity of the electoral process” as giving the court the power to intervene.
“The United States likewise suffers an injury when the certification of the election for a federal office is tainted by a frivolous candidacy because that undermines confidence in the make-up and workings of the federal government,” the lawsuit says.
Muller said he had never seen an attempt to use the introduction of the federal voter registration law in the way the DOJ is now.
“They’re just plucking from the preface and saying this gives them a free-wheeling right to enjoin operations in a state, and I just don’t think a court is going to buy that,” Muller said.
Under Alaska’s voting system, the top four candidates from the primary, regardless of party, advance to the general election. On the general election ballot, voters have the option to rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate gets a majority of first choice votes, voters’ other rankings come into play. In each round of the tabulation, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and their votes are reallocated to whoever those voters ranked next highest. That process continues until there’s a winner.
DOJ alleges there is a possibility that voters intending to cast ballots for the incumbent might not rank him at all, or will rank Daniel J. Sullivan over him, resulting in the challenger’s votes going to the Democratic candidate if the race goes into additional rounds of tabulation.
“Even if a majority of Alaskans wish to vote for Senator Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot will result in a victory for Peltola,” the lawsuit states.
However, a ranked-choice system could help reduce the impact of this kind of confusion.
Unlike in a traditional election where voters can only pick one candidate, an Alaska voter who wanted to vote for the incumbent could simply rank both Sullivans first and second, in any order. Assuming Peltola doesn’t win a majority of first choice votes, their vote would eventually go to the incumbent, who is likely to have much more support.
In June, ahead of the state’s primary, the Alaska state Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan should be included on the ballot after the state’s Division of Elections had removed him.
Muller noted that Alaska election officials “went out of their way” to reduce voter confusion, by including on the ballot the candidates’ middle initials, identifying Dan S. Sullivan as the incumbent, and leaving off the GOP party designation of the other Daniel Sullivan.
“This is friendly fire, this is suing Republicans in Alaska, I don’t know that is going to be taken well by state officials,” Muller said.
The administration is asking the court to declare unlawful the certification of a result that was “impacted by voter confusion” and to block election officials from certifying that result until there was an “investigation” into whether voters meaning to vote for the incumbent had cast ballots for other Sullivan.
“Alaska’s Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot,” a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. “Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”
But because ballots would be co-mingled, it is not clear how such an investigation would identify which voters may have cast ballots for a Dan Sullivan they didn’t intend to vote for, Muller noted.
“This is just the stuff that is just impossible to measure after the fact,” Muller said.
He also noted that there are numerous scenarios — such as a win by the Democrat outright without additional rounds of tabulation — which could make the lawsuit irrelevant. If not, Muller said, “there is a high likelihood” it is thrown out for legal reasons.

“No federal statute authorizes the relief the DOJ seeks and the Alaska Supreme Court has already concluded that this candidate will stay on ballot,” Gupta said. “The Constitution gives Alaska, not the US Justice Department, the authority over who’s on its ballot, how its votes are counted, and the certification of the election.”
Former Alaska state attorney general Bruce Botelho, a Democrat, called the lawsuit “unprecedented” and said that the Alaska Supreme Court’s previously consideration of the issue ” is the final word on interpretation of election Alaska election law.”
Alaska election officials expect to start the ranked-choice tabulation process on November 18, more than two weeks after Election Day, following the deadline for overseas ballots to arrive.
The new case has been assigned Judge Sharon L. Gleason, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. The administration has not yet made any emergency requests for the court to take an immediate action.

Ginsberg also noted that, like a recent DOJ lawsuit seeking the segregation of California ballots, this case was filed by the office of a political appointee in Washington that does not normally spearhead this type of litigation.
“I think they must have a client who is demanding it,” Ginsberg said. “There is not a rational legal reason to do it.”

Alaska does have a ranked-choice voting system which does allow voters to select both candidates on a ballot if they are confused.
Big picture view:
The DOJ lawsuit seeks emergency relief ahead of the Nov. 3 election, warning of potential "harm to the integrity" of the contest if the state certifies the results with both names on the ballot.
The Source: This story was written with information provided by The Associated Press. This story was reported from Orlando.

sources.text:
The Trump administration has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses while another candidate with the same name is on the ballot. That’s sparking fears of a lengthy battle between the U.S. government and states over certifying an election where President Donald Trump’s party is struggling.
In Ohio, the backlash over a campaign advertisement attacking Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, has spread beyond the state’s borders. The ad features Acton’s estranged mother calling her “a liar.”
Trump posted on social media Thursday that Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad was “hitting pay dirt” and that Acton was “fair game.”
Trump’s aggressive defense of Ramaswamy practically guarantees that more of his party’s candidates will face questions about the issue. Acton’s mother lost custody of her children after her husband was indicted for raping Acton.
Here’s the latest:
DCCC targets nonwhite voters with new digital ads across 42 districts
House Democrats’ campaign arm has unveiled five new digital ads targeting 42 districts across 20 states where nonwhite voters will help determine outcomes. The $1 million ad campaign, shared first with The Associated Press, hits Republicans on inflation, especially on gas and groceries, and on Trump’s aggressive immigration tactics.
Latino voters are seeing an add titled, “Pledge,” depicting federal agents’ mass deportation efforts and a voiceover saying, “Republicans broke their promise to America.”
Asian American and Pacific Islander voters are targeted with an ad about grocery prices, while young AAPI voters will see a distinct 15-second clip.
Black voters are seeing a spot on gas prices featuring Trump saying, “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation.”
The ads will reach Republican-held and Democratic-held districts in Alabama, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Florida, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Nebraska, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia.
Trump exempts some Canadian products from tariffs as he looks to boost Susan Collins
Collins is the only Republican senator from New England and is running against Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine.
The White House said products including plywood sheets, packing crates and some kinds of machinery would be exempted from the 50% tariffs that were applied to Canadian products earlier this year.
Collins said in a statement that the exemption is important because many farmers in the state “rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”
Trump, Kennedy announce ‘America First Seafood’ initiative
The president called the health secretary on stage in Florida as he talked about what the administration calls its ‘America First Seafood Strategy’ intended to boost U.S. fisheries.
According to the White House, the U.S. Department of Agriculture will make $5 billion in guaranteed loans “to expand American dominance in modernized meat and seafood processing.”
The administration also is:
1. launching Seafood.gov as a “one-stop destination for U.S. fishermen and consumers.”
2. introducing a voluntary “U.S. Caught Seafood” label, accessible for download on the website, to identify seafood caught and harvested by U.S. fishers.
The White House specifically cited the intended boost to Maine’s lobster industry.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins is locked in a tight battle for reelection in Maine. The seat is critical to determining control of the Senate when the new Congress convenes in January.
Trump has wrapped up rally for Republican candidates in South Florida
For 90 minutes, the president rolled through a list of his administration’s accomplishments, imploring voters, “you must vote Republican” in the midterm elections.
He also called on the crowd to back GOP candidates in the state’s contests, particularly U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, and Sen. Ashley Moody.
This weekend, Trump’s midterm campaign blitz heads to Georgia and Michigan, home of two of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.
Moody, Donalds praise Trump—even as Donalds walks a fine line on the economy
Trump called Moody and Donalds to the stage separately and both praised the president for his job performance and his support for their campaigns.
Moody urged Floridians to help Republicans hold majorities on Capitol Hill to “continue that fight for you.”
“It’s like a UFC fight on the White House lawn,” she said.
Donalds told Trump he was proud to support his presidential campaigns.
The congressman has carefully navigated the economic realities of Trump’s second presidency. He hasn’t blamed Trump for inflation but he’s built his general election bid around a promise to address Floridians’ economic struggles.
Even standing next to the president, he promised to make Florida “more affordable.”
Trump hails spending to boost nursing home work force
The president says his administration will spend $250 million to boost the nursing home work force in underserved areas.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Friday that it would dedicate $100 million, less than the figure the president quoted, with states committing $175 million for total program of $275 million.
The initiative is expected to support 4,000 nurses nationwide. Nursing students and licensed nurses will qualify for up to $40,000 in student loan repayment or a $10,000 stipend in exchange for a three-year-commitment to serve in a qualifying nursing home in a rural area or another area with a nursing labor shortage.
The money will come from civil penalties collected by CMS and state Medicaid agencies from nursing homes.
The administration previously faced backlash for trying to cap student loan amounts for nurses, among some other professions. But a federal judge put those changes on hold in June.
Lawmakers push Pentagon to restore Ukraine Starshield access
A group of bipartisan lawmakers has urged the Pentagon immediately restore Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite internet system used to intercept Russian strikes.
In a letter released Friday, six Democrats and two Republicans told Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that he should “ensure that Ukrainian forces maintain access to satellite communications at speeds and service levels.”
They said in the letter dated Thursday that it should include “connectivity over Russian territory where necessary to support Ukraine’s lawful military operations.”
The release comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed restrictions. The Trump administration has offered conflicting explanations as to who is responsible for the slowdown in the Elon Musk-built satellite internet system.
Trump on Friday brushed off questions about the role Musk played in the disruptions and declined to comment on who ordered the restrictions.
Newsom rallies California Democrats in push to claim 5 additional US House seats
California Gov. Gavin Newsom told fellow Democrats “it’s all on the line” as he urged party members to help win five additional U.S. House seats to allow Democrats to claim the majority next year.
President “Donald Trump’s presidency ends as we know it on Nov. 3, as long as we do our job,” Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential contender, said to cheers at a San Francisco rally.
State voters last year approved new congressional district boundaries intended to tilt five additional seats to Democrats to thwart Trump’s maneuvers in Texas and other Republican states to gain more seats and maintain the GOP’s fragile hold on House control.
Referring to Trump’s GOP, Newsom said, “These guys are not screwing around and nor can we.”
Former House speaker Nancy Pelosi told the crowd “we now have to work to elect those five seats.”
“We have to get out there,” she implored the crowd.
Trump repeats slur to describe Somalia
