In a long diatribe against Rep. Ilhan Omar, Trump said the Minnesota Democrat who was born in Somalia came to the U.S. from “a shithouse country.”
Omar is a naturalized citizen whose family fled civil war when she was a child. They first went to Kenya and then came to the U.S. as refugees.
During his first presidency, Trump denied using the phrase “shithole countries” to describe Haiti and other African countries, as some of his former aides described.
He admitted in 2025 that he had, in fact, used the description for majority Black nations.
Trump has repeatedly disparaged Somali immigrants to the U.S., including Omar, and suggested she should be stripped of her congressional seat and her citizenship.
Under Trump, federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives.
Trump suggests US can ‘take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran’
That came after someone in the south Florida crowd shouted a question about Cuba as Trump talked about his administration’s actions in Venezuela and Iran.
As U.S. ships eventually return from Iran, Trump suggested that one of them could “stop about 50 yards off the coast, they’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send in (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio.”
Trump has previously said “Cuba’s gonna be next” in terms of intervention efforts abroad.
Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.
Issues related to Cuba are particularly closely followed in South Florida, where Trump is speaking Friday.
Senior Ukrainian negotiator says local humanitarian ceasefire with Russia will start on Oct. 27
Ukraine’s top negotiator involved in a humanitarian mission led by U.S. first lady Melania Trump told The Associated Press late Friday that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Oct. 27 — two days before the mission begins — and last several days.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian assistance in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. He added that the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
Trump opens Florida rally at Florida Gulf Coast University
“We love Florida,” Trump said as he opened an afternoon rally, celebrating that he’s back in his adopted home state.
He’s trying to boost Florida Sen. Ashley Moody as she seeks her first election after being appointed to the seat and Rep. Byron Donalds in his effort to be elected governor.
Trump opened by misrepresenting his 2024 vote totals, suggesting he got “millions and millions” more votes than any other candidate ever has.
Trump got more than 77 million votes in 2024. But Democrat Joe Biden got 81 million votes to defeat Trump in 2020.
Omar responds to Trump claim about her name
Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar is responding directly to Trump claiming that she has an entirely different name and will not be allowed to be a member of the House.
“Whenever the news turns bad, this creep reaches for one name: mine. So let’s make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar,” the congresswoman said in a social media post on X. “Maybe you should focus on what your VP’s real name is.”
Trump’s comments came in a Truth Social post.
Omar’s name has been listed in court records as such for nearly two decades. She sought two marriage licenses under her name, twice filed for divorce under that same name and has numerous traffic and parking tickets under her name. She is also registered to vote under the name.
From 2009 to 2017 she was married to a man named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. His last name is the one Trump now claims is her correct name. But in their marriage and divorce filings, she always used the name Ilhan Omar and did not adopt his name.
Greeting Trump, DeSantis says midterms ‘all about the turnout’ for Republicans
On the Southwest Florida International Airport tarmac as Trump landed Friday, GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis predicted wins for Republicans in tight Senate races as long as turnout is robust.
“If people come out, if our people vote, I think we’ll win, not just in Florida, but some of these other Senate races that are close,” DeSantis said, welcoming the president “back to his home state.”
As the president brings his midterm blitz to Florida, DeSantis said “no one does it better” than the president when it comes to energizing voters.
“If they vote, we’re going to win big,” Trump said.
According to an Associated Press analysis of early voting two weeks before Election Day, voter turnout is soaring compared with the last midterm election in many of the states expected to decide control of the U.S. Senate.
Trump says he ordered the Justice Department lawsuit over Alaska’s US Senate race
President Donald Trump said he told his administration to file a lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president’s party is struggling.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.
The lawsuit centers on one of the president’s longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republican fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what’s likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state’s former congresswoman.
The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.
Republican congressman from Iowa releases new video featuring Democratic supporters
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, a Republican, is emphasizing his bipartisan support in the final week of his reelection campaign. His new political advertisement includes some Democrats saying directly to camera that they’re backing Nunn over Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott, a state senator.
Nunn is seeking his third term representing the district that includes Des Moines, the fast-growing suburbs to the city’s west, and rural counties in southern Iowa. While Republicans outnumber Democrats in each of the three targeted House races in Iowa, Nunn’s has the smallest GOP advantage.
One member of the Des Moines city council identifies himself in the ad as a moderate Democrat who is ticket-splitting this year.
“I’m supporting Rob Sand, and I strongly support Zach Nunn,” Mike Simonson says in the ad. Sand is the Democrat running for governor.
Trump says Musk should not be blamed for Starshield disruption in Ukraine
Trump brushed off questions about the role Elon Musk played in disruptions to service between the satellite system he owns and the drones Ukraine uses to fight Russia.
“Elon will never do anything wrong,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “I know him very well. He’s a fair person.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that service remained slow from Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service. The disruption produced speed restrictions on Ukrainian drones, which have been unable to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones.
Trump said he hadn’t heard that there are still problems with the service, and declined to comment on who ordered the restrictions to Starshield, telling a reporter, “I wouldn’t tell you if I did know.”
Trump suggests NFL should postpone this weekend’s Paris game because of unrest
“The NFL could have probably postponed that match if you want to know,” Trump told reporters. “France is really in trouble, that’s what happens when you go left.”
Sunday’s game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints is scheduled to go ahead despite recent civil unrest in Paris and other cities in France. More demonstrations are planned for this weekend.
The protests in France were originally sparked by high school and university students demanding better school funding, smaller class sizes, and other reforms to the country’s education system, but have morphed into a broader outlet for public anger about rising costs and the government’s effort to tighten its budget.
While tens of millions have taken to the streets, some rioters have used the demonstrations as cover for looting and destroying government property.
Vivek Ramaswamy defends ad accusing Amy Acton of lying
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy accused his opponent in the Ohio governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton, of lying about the ad he’s running, which features her mother calling her “a liar.”
“The irony is they’re lying about an ad that is about lying,” Ramaswamy said.
Speaking at a campaign stop in Strongsville, Ohio, he added that the ad had “nothing to do” with childhood abuse. Acton’s mother lost custody of her children after her husband was indicted for raping Acton.
“They’re changing the subject,” Ramaswamy said, “because they don’t want to answer for their own failures.”
The advertisement also includes Acton’s mother insinuating her daughter has mental health issues. Acton is Ohio’s former public health director and has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.
Acton has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad.
“I won’t normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I’m complaining about,” she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio.
Judge allows Trump’s tree cutting at a historic DC golf course to resume
The historic public golf course at East Potomac Park is one of several Trump projects in D.C. that are embroiled in lawsuits challenging the president’s remake of the city. Trump wants to turn it into a professional-level course.
On Thursday evening, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes denied a request to extend her temporary order that had stopped the National Park Service from cutting more trees at the park.
Reyes ordered the halt on Oct. 13, after a holiday weekend when the government, with little notice, cut down more than 400 trees with plans to cut hundreds more. The actions led to eight hours of court hearings.
Plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to block Trump’s renovation had sought to extend the stoppage. The order lapses Oct. 26, and Trump has said work would begin “immediately” on the course.
Trump doubles down on support for Ramaswamy on ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother
Leaving the White House Friday, Trump said “no” when asked if he had reconsidered his support for the Ohio campaign advertisement attacking Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton, following criticism from other Republicans.
The president engaged in a heated exchange with a reporter asking if the president knew about the backstory behind the ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The spot features Acton’s mother, who lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
“You don’t know that,” Trump said, of the abuse allegations, adding that Acton’s mother had an “obligation” to tell voters “that her daughter is a liar.”
Zelenskyy urges trilateral talks with Trump and Putin
The Ukrainian president said he spoke with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner just before appearing remotely for an address at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank.
Witkoff and Zelenskyy met earlier this week in Oslo, Norway, about ways to end Russia’s war in Ukraine before Witkoff went on to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
Putin says he agreed to trilateral talks next month with Trump and Zelenskyy, who on Friday said “we need these meetings, and we need diplomacy to move forward.”
Zelenskyy says we “cannot have these meetings without America” and that Ukraine was counting on the U.S. to “give this priority at every level.”
He said reaching a “ceasefire is point number one” and then after that would be sorting out security guarantees. Russian officials have resisted a ceasefire and said they want to broker a comprehensive settlement to end the war.
Trump says Republicans aren’t losing in Mississippi
The president has a rather eyebrow-raising addition to his midterm travel schedule: a stop Monday in deep-red Mississippi, where GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is up for reelection.
Asked about the visit Friday, Trump said he won the state by 32 points and “they’ve asked me to go,” without specifying who “they” were.
“I look forward to it. And Cindy Hyde-Smith, you know, Cindy Hyde is fantastic,” Trump said. “She’s very popular. She’s up in the polls. She’s not losing.”
Trump to vote this weekend in Florida
The president is an early voter.
“I think we’re voting tomorrow in Florida,” Trump told reporters as he was preparing to depart for a rally in Fort Myers and a weekend in Palm Beach, where his club is located.
Early voting in Palm Beach County began Monday and runs through Nov. 1.
At another point in the gaggle with journalists, Trump was asked about this year’s early voting figures and which party that benefited.
“Nobody knows,” he responded.
___

This move has sparked concerns about a lengthy battle between the U.S. government and states over election certification. The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit Thursday, demanding Alaska be blocked from certifying a win for Democrat Mary Peltola if the other Sullivan remains on the ballot.

Trump DOJ Sues to Block Senate Race Results if Republican Loses
The Trump administration is already meddling in the midterm elections.
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan speaks during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate with his opponent, former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola, on September 12.
Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan speaks during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate with his opponent, former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola, on September 12.
The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit to block Alaska from certifying its Senate election results in the event that Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. This move is the Trump administration’s most blatant effort to swing ballots in Republicans’ favor this November.
The lawsuit alleges that the Senate election should be nullified if Sullivan loses because there’s another “Daniel J. sources.news_title: Citing preamble to NVRA, DOJ sues to enjoin certification of Alaska's Senate race (it won't go anywhere) #ELB
sources.text:
The Department of Justice has filed United States v. Alaska in federal court. The gist of the case is this: there’s a risk of voter confusion from having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot, and the State of Alaska should not be permitted to certify its results “pending an investigation” to determine whether any votes cast for the one Sullivan were meant for another.
The case isn’t yet ripe, obviously, but the Department is pre-suing both to signal to the public that it’s “doing something” and that it’s ready if the result goes against the GOP in the state. And of course it probably would have helped Alaska if the Department thought about weighing in months and months ago, when there was feasibility in assisting with respect to the remedy.
Such factual investigation is essentially impossible (the best evidence that voters preferred one Sullivan over another is how they marked their ballots) and a reason why parties bring ballot access cases before the ballots are printed rather than after, so such a factual caveat is largely meaningless.
But setting aside the factual issue, the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen. It cites the preamble to the National Voter Registration Act–its “findings and purposes”–as the source of law for the claim. That part reads, “The purposes of this chapter are . . . to protect the integrity of the electoral process.” 52 U.S.C. § 20501(b)(3).
The Department excised the “The purposes of this chapter are” language throughout its complaint and replaced it with something not in the statute. For instance, it claims that certifying the result “would violate Defendants’ duties under the NVRA to ‘protect
the integrity of the electoral process.'” That is certainly not what the NVRA does. This language places no “duties” on a state outside of those enumerated in the chapter. And, of course, the Department cannot find any ballot access rules in the chapter.
I also cannot imagine anything some election litigators in the Republican Party might want less than to open this language of the NVRA to freewheeling litigation around the United States in future elections.
Some, in a panic, might react that the Department is trying to deny certification of an election in a state. Of course that’s what the Department is trying to do. But the legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success. (I write essentially because, of course, one never knows how one judge or two judges on a panel might react, but I think the Supreme Court will have nothing for this claim.)
In short, like many Department letters over the last few years, it is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation. This one simply takes the form of a complaint.
(Note: I write “enjoin” in the title because the case is captioned as declaratory and injunctive relief, but the prayer for relief does not ask for an injunction because Paragraph 44 is missing the verb asking the court to take action. Paragraph 43 asks for declaratory relief.)

sources.news_title: Trump admin seeks to block Alaska Senate result if Dan Sullivan loses
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Friday he told the Department of Justice to sue the state of Alaksa and its election officials over its U.S. Senate ballot which includes two candidates named Dan Sullivan.
"I'm the one that said 'do it,'" Trump told reporters as he arrived in Florida Friday afternoon.
The Trump administration has said it aims to stop Alaska from certifying the Senate race result if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, amid concern votes for another candidate named Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome of the ranked-choice vote.
A lawsuit filed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday against the state of Alaska and various election officials alleges that the Republican candidate listed on the ranked-choice ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race intending to mislead voters into backing him instead of the incumbent with the same name.
"So, the Democrats put up a guy, I don't think he ever voted before, all of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate," Trump said. "The Daniel J. is the fake and he wants to change his middle initial to "S," and he says this has nothing to do with politics."
Speaking later at his rally, Trump said, "That's not so dumb. Actually, it's cheating like hell."
Trump has repeatedly accused Democrats of planting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, to confuse Alaska voters. In a social media post earlier this week, Trump—who has endorsed the incumbent—called his presence on the ballot a "scam" that could threaten Senator Dan Sullivan's potential victory in what has become one of the closest Senate contests this year.
"Even 1, 2, or 3 percent could make the difference," the president wrote. "Dan S. Sullivan is leading by a lot, but this is CHEATING in an Election, and the Judge that allowed this to happen should be ashamed of himself."
Senator Dan Sullivan is currently 2.7 points behind Peltola, according to VoteHub's poll tracker, underscoring how potentially consequential even a small number of votes could be.
A spokesperson for Peltola's campaign told Newsweek Friday, "This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan’s allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he’ll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans' expense for over a decade.
"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," the spokesperson said.
Why the DOJ is Suing Alaska
Dan J. Sullivan was a member of the Alaska Independence Party until it dissolved late last year, only registering as a Republican when he filed his candidacy in the Senate race earlier this year.
Alaska election officials initially agreed that the retired teacher’s filing was intended to confuse voters and sought to exclude him from the ballot. But an Alaska trial court ruled against that exclusion and the Alaska Supreme Court summarily affirmed that decision, putting Dan J. Sullivan back on the ballot.
The lawsuit hinges on whether the votes cast for the "decoy" Sullivan, a retired teacher, would have changed the winner under Alaska’s ranked choice voting system if they had instead been cast for the Trump-endorsed incumbent.
It would also require an investigation into whether Alaskans who cast their vote for Dan J. Sullivan actually intended to vote for the incumbent, and it would allow further procedures to determine what the election result would have been without the alleged voter confusion.
“Alaska’s Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot," a DOJ spokesperson told Newsweek. "Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”
Newsweek contacted the White House, Alaska Division of Elections, and both Sullivans’ campaigns for comment by email on Friday morning, outside of standard working hours.
What Election Experts Think of the DOJ Lawsuit
“The lawsuit is based on very real and valid concerns about voter confusion,” Michael Morley, the Sheila M. McDevitt Professor of Law and Faculty Director of the Election Law Center at the Florida State University, told Newsweek.
“The Alaska secretary of state concluded Daniel J. Sullivan is not an actual good-faith candidate but rather was running only to confuse or mislead voters. Having said that, the DOJ’s lawsuit is completely meritless,” he added.
The DOJ sued under the National Voter Registration Act, Morley said, but does not even allege that the statute has been violated here. “Rather, the DOJ is claiming that allowing the election’s results to be impacted by a sham candidacy would undermine the law’s purpose. That’s not a valid basis for suing,” the professor said.
“Moreover, any concerns about the sham candidacy could have been raised before the election, before votes were cast. Indeed, Alaska courts refused to allow election officials to remove him from the ballot,” Morley added.
The professor believes the lawsuit will be “quickly” dismissed. “If Senator Dan S. Sullivan loses, and Daniel J. Sullivan’s vote tally exceeds the margin of victory, then the senator’s best bet would be to file an election contest with the U.S. Senate, which is the sole judge of its members’ elections and returns. The Senate can decide for itself whether to accept such results.”
Professor Mark Brown, of Capital University School of Law, agrees. “No federal statute authorizes the relief the DOJ seeks and the Alaska Supreme Court has already concluded that Dan J. Sullivan was illegally under Alaska—and federal—law removed from the ballot,” he told Newsweek. “The Alaska Supreme Court thus restored his name to the ballot. DOJ's lawsuit is frivolous.”
How Are the Two Sullivans Running for the Alaska Senate Race?
Six years ago, Alaska narrowly passed a ballot measure shifting the state to a ranked choice voting system allowing voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
Ballot Measure 2, which got 50.55 percent of the vote in 2020, created the non-partisan primary and the four-candidate ranked choice voting general election that The Last Frontier is now using.
Under this system, which Alaska shares with only one other state in the country, Maine, the top four candidates from each respective primary in the state earlier this year, whether for governor, the House or the Senate, are set to appear on the ballot on November 3, regardless of party affiliation. Voters have the option to rank them in order of preference, though they can also choose one candidate only if they prefer so.
A candidate who receives more than 50 percent of first-choice votes wins outright. If no one passes this threshold, then the candidate who comes in last place is eliminated, and those who selected that candidate first will have their second-choice vote counted. The process continues until one candidate gets more than 50 percent of the vote.
This system is why four candidates are on the ballot in the Alaska Senate race, including Democrat Mary Peltola and Republicans Sen. Dan Sullivan, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., and Gerald Heikes.
The Trump administration, in the DOJ lawsuit filed Thursday, claimed that "the sole purpose of [Dan J. Sullivan’s] candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan."
In June, when Dan J. Sullivan was reinstated on the ballot, the retired teacher and fishing enthusiast said that he is running because he is disappointed with Sullivan’s representation and wants change for the state.
"It’s a free country," he said, as reported by Courthouse News Service. "Most Alaskans are proud Independents and it’s my sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters’ intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running."
The newly published ballots show that Alaska election officials have come to something of a solution to solve the debate around the two Sullivans. The ballots list incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan as a "Registered Republican" and mark him as the "Incumbent." The retired teacher appears under his full name, "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.," without a party designation displayed beneath his name.
A Key Race for Control of the Senate
Democrats have a chance to seize control of the Senate in the midterms, with Republicans currently holding a narrow 53-47 majority.
While most of the seats up for grabs in the upper chamber are in states where Trump has won by comfortable margins in 2024, the unpopular war in Iran and rising inflation in recent months have turned many of these races into unexpectedly competitive ones.
Alaska, a state which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, has now become a key battleground in the fight for control of the upper chamber, with Peltola gaining ground over the Republican incumbent.
Building on voters’ growing anger over higher prices, Peltola—an Alaskan who supports oil, gas and gun rights—has focused her campaign on the cost of living, trying to appeal to moderate Republicans disappointed with the Trump administration and independents as well as Democrats. Polls show that her strategy may be working.
Who Is Leading the Latest Polls?
With less than two weeks ahead of Election Day, every poll released this month gives Peltola a narrow but consistent lead over Sullivan, while the other two candidates typically receive less than 5 percent of the vote in the first round.
A poll released by progressive pollster Data for Progress earlier this month and conducted between October 8 and October 16 among 675 likely voters, gives Peltola ahead with 49 percent of the vote while Sullivan had 46 percent of the vote in the first round of the election. Dan J. Sullivan had 4 percent of the vote and Heikes only 1 percent. In the final round, Peltola’s lead had grown to 51 percent to Sullivan’s 49 percent. The poll had a margin of error of ±4 percentage points.
The Democratic candidate received 48 percent of the vote in an InsiderAdvantage poll conducted between October 9 and October 10, while Sullivan had 43 percent of the vote in a four-way ballot. Dan J. Sullivan Jr. and Heikes received 1.7 percent and 2.2 percent of the vote, respectively, while 5.3 percent of likely voters were undecided.
In the second round of voting, without Dan J. Sullivan and Heikes, 50.1 percent of the vote went to Peltola and 48.0 percent to the incumbent. The poll was conducted among 1,200 likely voters and had margin of error of ±2.83 percentage points.
Americans Want Trump to Accept Outcome of Midterms
A new YouGov survey shows that an overwhelming majority of Americans want the president and his administration to accept the outcome of the midterm elections, no matter the result. According to the poll, conducted on October 22, 2026, among 8,694 U.S. adults, 71 percent of Americans think Trump should "accept the results" if Republicans lose their majority in the U.S. House.
The opinion is bipartisan: 87 percent of Democrats, 67 percent of Independents, and 61 percent of Republicans said the same. Only 8 percent of all voters said Trump should not accept the results, while 21 percent said they were not sure.
YouGov has not released a similar poll on the Senate.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton, Trevor Davies, Dan Gooding and Emma Lee-Sang
Update 10/23/26, 10:18 a.m. ET: This article was updated with comment from Michael Morley and Mark Brown.

sources.news_title: Trump administration files unusual lawsuit against Alaska that seeks to block upset that could cost Republican control of Congress.
sources.text:
Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for our free weekly newsletter to get the latest.
The U.S. Department of Justice late Thursday filed an unusual lawsuit against the state of Alaska seeking to block certification of its U.S. Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses.
With early voting underway in the contest that could determine partisan control of the Senate, and polls showing a tight race between incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, the Trump administration is laying the groundwork to challenge the Alaska results in some circumstances.
The lawsuit centers on the participation of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot, something that the Justice Department said is likely to confuse Alaska voters.
Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and former member of the Alaskan Independence Party who switched his registration to Republican shortly before entering the Senate race, is one of four candidates for the seat.
Alaska election officials disqualified Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot in June, but the former teacher challenged the decision. Sullivan rejected any suggestion he was working with Democrats to dilute the vote for Sen. Sullivan and said he ran because he was dissatisfied with the incumbent’s track record. The Alaska Supreme Court ultimately sided with the former teacher and cleared the way for him to be on the ballot.
Alaska’s ballot includes the word “incumbent” next to Sen. Sullivan’s name, but the Justice Department filing argues that the other Dan Sullivan’s presence on the ballot “threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan.”
In its lawsuit, the Justice Department said results may be tainted by voter confusion “if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”
In such a case, the Justice Department wants a federal judge to stop election officials from certifying the election “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”
Legal scholars said the lawsuit appears to have little chance of succeeding.
“It arises from real, valid, recognized concerns about a bad-faith sham candidate, potential confusion, and effective disenfranchisement,” Michael Morley, an election law expert at Florida State University said in an email. “But this particular lawsuit is frivolous and will be quickly dismissed.”
Morley said “any concerns about the sham candidacy could have been raised before the election, before votes were cast,” and that the Senate itself could challenge the results and refuse to seat Peltola if she wins.
Ilya Somin, a constitutional law professor at George Mason University and scholar at the libertarian Cato Institute, also said the lawsuit appeared to be baseless.
“Any law suppressing candidates based on potential voter confusion would violate the First Amendment,” he said in an email.
“As to why DOJ waited so long, I don’t know,” he said. “Maybe this is one of those politically motivated cases they brought only after pressure from on high overruled line attorneys.”
President Donald Trump took credit for the lawsuit on Friday.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters.
Alaska uses ranked choice voting, which means results could take time
The lawsuit is part of a concerted Justice Department effort to inject more federal control over elections, which are the responsibility of state and local officials. Last week, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit in California that seeks to compel the state to segregate as many as 20,000 ballots it says could be cast by noncitizens. California officials say that lawsuit is based on flawed assertions that some registered voters are noncitizens, and legal scholars have said that the Trump administration is unlikely to succeed.
If Peltola wins in Alaska, she would be the first Democrat in 18 years to represent the state in the Senate. The race is expected to be close.
In addition, Alaska is one of two states — the other is Maine — using ranked choice voting to select a winner in a Senate race this year. In Alaska, voters will rank the four U.S. Senate candidates by preference. If none of them win more than 50% of first-choice votes at the outset, Alaska will then shift on Nov. 18th to the ranked choice voting process.
At that point, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their supporters’ votes will be redistributed to those voters’ second choices. That means that if Daniel J. Sullivan is eliminated, his votes could then go to Sen. Sullivan, depending on how the voter ranked the candidates.
The process continues until one candidate secures a majority.
Even if the Justice Department lawsuit fails, members of the U.S. Senate could try to prevent Peltola from taking the seat. There are some precedents for that.
In 1975, the Senate declined to seat either candidate in a disputed New Hampshire election, eventually declaring the seat vacant and paving the way for a new election. In another case, the Senate overturned the results of a 1924 Iowa election and seated the losing candidate nearly two years later.
“If Senator Dan S. Sullivan loses, and Daniel J. Sullivan’s vote tally exceeds the margin of victory, then the senator’s best bet would be to file an election contest with the U.S. Senate, which is the sole judge of its members’ elections and returns,” Morley said.
Dion Nissenbaum is Votebeat’s senior national reporter and is based in Houston. Contact Dion at dnissenbaum@votebeat.org.

sources.news_title: DOJ sues Alaska to block Senate race certification if Republican loses
sources.text:
The Department of Justice filed an extraordinary lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the winner of its upcoming U.S. Senate election if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The lawsuit cites what it argues is likely voter confusion from the name of another candidate, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot.
The DOJ says that could help Democratic nominee Mary Peltola defeat the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, in what is expected to be a close contest. The Alaska race is one of several Senate contests in November that could determine whether Republicans retain their slim majority in the upper chamber of Congress.
“The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” says the suit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Alaska. In addition to the state, the complaint names Alaska Elections Division Director Carol Beecher, the state’s election boards and the state Ballot Counting Review Board as defendants.
The suit asks a federal judge in Alaska to bar the state from certifying “any result that may be impacted by voter confusion … pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”
The suit alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan’s “sole purpose” of running for the Senate “is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.” Sullivan first registered as a Republican earlier this year. He previously was a member of the Alaska Independence Party.
The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the Alaska Senate race as one of seven “toss-up” contests for that chamber. The election tracking site FiftyPlusOne‘s average of polling shows Peltola, a former U.S. House member from Alaska, with just a two-point lead over Sullivan.
The suit came hours after President Donald Trump, in a Truth Social post, wrote, “I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing, with the Dumocrats putting up another man, totally unrelated to Politics, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.”
“It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM. Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference,” Trump said.
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness.”
Alaska’s general election for the Senate uses ranked-choice voting. Voters rank their candidates in order of preference. If no candidate gets more than 50% in round one, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated in the second round, and that process continues until there are just two candidates and the winner is the one with the most votes.
“Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan,” the suit says. “For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan.”
“Other supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola,” the suit says. “They might not rank Senator Sullivan at all, resulting in votes for Daniel J. Sullivan to be transferred to Peltola after Daniel J. Sullivan’s all-but-guaranteed elimination in the first or second round of tabulations.”
In a statement to CNBC, a DOJ spokesperson said, “Alaska’s Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot.”
“Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters,” the spokesperson said.
Nate Adams, the campaign spokesman for Sen. Sullivan, said, “We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course.”
“Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he’ll keep building on for the next six years,” Adams said.
CNBC has requested comment from Alaska’s attorney general, Daniel J. Sullivan and Peltola.
Devan Barber, director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, in a statement to CNBC said, “Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses.”
Daniel J. Sullivan originally was blocked from the state’s primary ballot in June, after the Alaska Division of Elections said his candidacy declaration was no properly filed, and because of a finding that the candidacy was aimed at duping voters who planned to vote for Sen. Sullivan.
Among the reasons the division cited were Daniel J. Sullian’s intention to use the name “Dan Sullivan” on the ballot, his request to be designated as affiliated with the Republican Party on the ballot, and his work with a political consultant who is “a known longtime supporter of Decmoratic candidates,” including Peltola, the lawsuit notes.
Daniel J. Sullivan was added to the ballot after asking a trial court judge to review the decision’s determination. The Alaska Supreme Court later upheld that decision.
Daniel J. Sullivan received just 2.5% of the vote in Alaska’s open primary on Aug. 28, but that was enough to win him one of four spots on the Senate general election ballot.
Peltola got 49.5% in the primary, and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, received just 1.1% of the primary vote, earning him the fourth spot on the ballot.
Although Daniel J. Sullivan sought to run as a Republican, the Division of Elections decided not to list that party next to his name on the general election ballot. His name is spelled out, “Daniel J. Sullivan,” and there are no other words on that line.
Both Sen. Sullivan, who has been in the Senate since 2015, and Heikes have the words “registered Republican” in parentheses next to their names.
And Sen. Sullivan, listed on the ballot as Dan. S. Sullivan, also has the word “incumbent” next to his name.
— CNBC’s Justin Papp contributed to this article.

What’s the Legal Basis for DOJ Blocking Alaska Election Certification?
The legal basis for the DOJ’s lawsuit rests on the argument that certifying an election with a confusingly named candidate violates constitutional protections for fair elections. Can the DOJ Actually Stop a State from Certifying Election Results?

The federal government has the authority to sue states over election practices when it believes federal constitutional protections are being violated. This is similar to other instances where states face federal legal challenges, such as when Ags From 24 States Threaten To Sue Over Joe Bidens policies. However, the DOJ’s request here is explicitly limited. It only seeks to block certification if Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses and if the votes for Daniel J. Sullivan would have changed the outcome. If the incumbent wins outright, the suit does not seek to block certification.
This narrow focus suggests the administration is concentrated on protecting the incumbent Republican rather than addressing voter confusion more broadly. The conditional nature of the injunction makes this a highly unusual legal strategy.

Election officials across the country may face increased scrutiny over ballot design and candidate qualifications. The case could also encourage more preemptive federal lawsuits in close races.
